source_text: Vel quid prodest eius rei modestia, cuius accusat se ipsa praesentia? Vide ergo quo tua acumina provehantur. Primo, quia peccat natura sine voluntate; quod non potest. Secundo, quia est peccatum, et non peccat, id est, una res est, et non est. Deinde, quando turbat pacem, miserabilis est, nec pro tanto crimine plectitur dissipatae quietis; quando autem perficit iniquitatem, damnabilis est. Sed lex peccati sicut meretur ipsa tormentum, ita excusat hominis voluntatem. Quia lex et cogens, et naturalis, et numquam recedens, superari utique a voluntate non potest; et nemo propter hoc reus est, quod vitare non potuit. Sed nec ipsa lex peccat, quia aliud facere non potuit. Deus autem inevitabilia reatui adscribit; nec ut hoc tantum mali faciat, ab ullo cogitur; omnibus igitur absolutis, hic solus in crimine reperitur, qui mira fronte imputat aliis necessitatem, cum ipse sine necessitate delinquat. Macte virtute prudentiae, nobilissime disputator, qui gradibus Punicae dialexeos, ut commendares dona, evertisti iudicia; ut simulares gratiam, subruisti iustitiam; ut infamares naturam, criminatus es hominum Conditorem; et ita criminatus es, ut non solum aliquo peccatore, sed ipsa lege peccati Deus tuus nocentior appareret. Et post haec profanissime catholicis sacerdotibus convicium facis, ut dicas eos negare gratiam Christi, cuius aequitatem tuentur; cum nos laudemus quidem clementiam remediorum, sed legum manente iustitia.
pass_a_gloss: Or what does the moderation of that thing profit, whose presence itself accuses? See therefore where your sharp points are carried. First, because nature sins without will; which cannot. Second, because there is sin, and it does not sin, that is, one thing is, and is not. Then, when it disturbs peace, it is miserable, nor is it punished for so great a crime of dissipated quiet; but when it completes iniquity, it is damnable. But the law of sin as it itself deserves torment, so it excuses the will of the human. Because a law both compelling, and natural, and never receding, cannot at any rate be overcome by will; and no one is guilty on account of this, which he could not avoid. But neither does the law itself sin, because it could not do another thing. But God ascribes inevitable things to guilt; nor is he forced by anyone that he do this so great an evil; all therefore having been absolved, this one alone is found in the charge, who with a wondrous forehead imputes necessity to others, when he himself offends without necessity. Hail to the virtue of prudence, most noble disputant, who by the steps of Punic dialectic, that you might commend gifts, overturned judgments; that you might simulate grace, undermined justice; that you might defame nature, charged the Founder of humans; and so charged him, that not only than some sinner, but than the law of sin itself your God would appear more noxious. And after these things most profanely you make insult to catholic priests, that you say they deny the grace of Christ, whose equity they guard; when we indeed praise the clemency of remedies, but with the justice of the laws remaining.

lemmas.lexica: LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: Or what good is moderation in something whose very presence accuses it? See where your clever distinctions take you. First, nature sins without will, which is impossible. Second, it is sin and does not sin: the same thing both is and is not. Next, when it disturbs peace it is miserable, but is not punished for so great a crime as destroying tranquillity; when it carries out injustice, however, it merits condemnation. Yet the law of sin, just as it itself deserves torment, excuses the human will. A law that compels, is natural, and never departs certainly cannot be overcome by will; no one is guilty for what he could not avoid. But the law itself does not sin either, because it could not do anything else. God, however, counts unavoidable things as guilt, and no one compels him to commit so great an evil. Everyone else is therefore acquitted, and he alone is found guilty: with astonishing effrontery he imputes necessity to others while himself doing wrong without necessity.

Well done for your wise virtue, most noble debater! By the steps of African dialectic, to commend gifts you have overturned judgments; to pretend grace you have overthrown justice; to defame nature you have accused humanity's Creator. You have accused him in such a way that your God appears more guilty not only than some sinner but than the very law of sin. After this you most profanely insult catholic priests, saying that they deny the grace of Christ whose fairness they defend. We praise the mercy of the remedies, but maintain the justice of the laws (compare Romans 7:23).

choices.why: Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
